The phenomenon: iterative degradation ("generation loss")

It's the photocopy-of-a-photocopy effect: every editing pass introduces minor, often imperceptible artifacts, and when an output is fed back in for subsequent edits, those artifacts accumulate into visible degradation — static noise, tint shifts, scatter points; after roughly 5–10 steps models start failing visibly, and even instruction-following deteriorates. First, the honest read of your attached frames, because they diagnose exactly why the style system is the missing layer — then the plan, the style build, the audio anchors, and the bible fix.

What the frames reveal

The scenes are charming — but they expose two drifts that a style system exists to prevent:

Medium drift: your characters were built as photographed handcrafted puppets (real casing, real doll wigs, real glass). In these video frames they've become smooth CG/Pixar figures — Kati most of all: she's gained human anatomy (smooth articulated legs, crossed knees, human proportions), her dress became soft leather-fabric rather than carved peel, her face is now an animated-film face. Rolf survived best (casing speckle intact, wig reads); Bert is mid-drift (foam went cotton-wool, but held). The video models' prior is "cute 3D animation," and without a style anchor they pull every generation toward it.

Design drift: details migrating — Kati's peel-dress logic gone, Bert's coaster feet became a glass pedestal foot. Small per-shot, compounding per-season.

Neither is fatal — but you must now make one deliberate decision the whole system hangs on: is the show's canon look (A) the strict puppet-prop photography of the character sheets, or (B) this softer miniature-CG hybrid the video models naturally produce? My honest recommendation: (A) as the target, accepting ~15% drift — it's more distinctive, ownable, and consistent with your anchors; pure (B) makes you look like every AI-Pixar channel. But it's a taste call, and everything below works for either — you just have to pick the north star once.

The overall architecture (five layers)

Your uploaded skill files already form the middle of a system; here's the complete machine:

CHARACTER LAYER ✅ done — bibles (personality+voice), sheets, master prompts, per-character anchors.

STYLE LAYER ⬅ the gap this plan fills — the show's world identity: one style bible + style block + style anchor images, governing every frame regardless of which character/tool.

STORY LAYER ✅ your 3 skills (story selector → screenplay → prompt writer) — needs the dialogue fix (below) fed into it.

PRODUCTION LAYER — per-tool guidelines (your Omni/Seedance docs) + the anchor kit each generation carries: character image refs + style ref + voice anchor + verbatim blocks (Voice Line, Style Block).

REVIEW LAYER — the design-review gates, now extended with a style gate: every clip judged against the style anchors before it enters an episode.

The research consensus for serialized AI content matches what you already discovered building characters: consistency comes from rigorous prompt discipline + detailed bibles reused verbatim + reference anchors in every generation — the same trinity, now applied at show level instead of character level.

Building the Style Layer (your core question)

This is your film project's style_dna.json practice, applied to the show. Five steps:

Step 1 — Write the style pillars (one page, decided once). Draft, based on everything locked so far:

World rule: everything is handcrafted and miniature — sets are miniature dioramas of real materials (real wood loungers, real terrycloth towels, real water), photographed like tabletop film sets. The frames you attached already gesture at this (the tiny bench, real towel) — that's the show's world: a miniature Germany built by hand.

Camera rule: macro/tabletop photography feel — shallow depth of field, slight tilt-shift miniature quality, eye-level-with-the-puppet framing.

Light rule: soft naturalistic daylight or warm interior practicals; never flat studio grey in scenes (that's reserved for the sheets), never neon-CG gloss.

Material rule (the anti-Pixar clause): every surface answers "what real material is this" — matte food textures, visible fabric weave, no smooth vinyl skin, no articulated doll joints.

Grade rule: one LUT/grade applied in Premiere/Resolve to every clip — the cheapest and most reliable unifier you own, and it's already your pipeline's final step.

Step 2 — Generate 3–5 style anchor plates. Empty scenes, no characters: the Biergarten table, the U-Bahn platform, the supermarket Pfand machine, the flat's kitchen — generated once at high quality in the locked style, gated, saved as style_anchor_01..05. These are for the world what the character sheets are for the cast.

Step 3 — Extract the STYLE BLOCK — a fixed paragraph, verbatim in every video prompt, sibling of the Voice Line:

STYLE: A handcrafted miniature puppet world — real-material food puppets 
photographed on miniature diorama sets, macro tabletop-photography feel, 
shallow depth of field, soft natural light, matte realistic textures on 
every surface. Handmade prop realism, not smooth 3D animation, not 
cartoon.

(Tune wording once against test generations, then freeze it. Never paraphrase between prompts — same rule as the Voice Lines.)

Step 4 — Bind references per generation (Seedance 2.0 is built for this): it takes up to 9 images, 3 videos, 3 audio refs with @-mention binding — so every scene generation carries: @character (sheet crop) + @style (the matching style anchor plate) + the Style Block + Voice Line in text. Once you have one perfect approved clip, it becomes a style video reference too — Seedance abstracts style and rhythm from reference video, which is the strongest anchor of all.

Step 5 — Style gate + grade. Every clip: two-second side-by-side against the style anchor; pass → grade with the show LUT → assemble. Drifted → regenerate before it infects an episode.

The audio reference system (research answer)

The workflow that works, and one critical expectation to set:

The caveat first: Seedance's audio reference guides acoustic characteristics, timing and rhythm — it does not clone the exact voice into the output; the model generates new audio sharing the reference's pacing and character. So the audio anchor's job is steering, and your existing relink-audio-in-post practice remains the precision guarantee.

The build (per character, once):

Generate the canonical voice in Flow with your locked voice + Customize Performance text (or Seed Audio, which is explicitly designed for reference-voice consistency and emotional direction — generate 5–10 sample lines and keep the reference stable forever after).

Script: ~15 seconds of German covering the character's emotional range (calm line + signature phrase + one emotional beat). Anchor scripts:
ROLF: Die Party ist okay. Die Musik ist gut, aber zu laut. Ich bleibe eine Stunde. Dann gehe ich. Egal.

BERT: Servus, meine Freunde! Ich habe eine geniale Idee! Zuerst trinken wir ein Bier — dann erkläre ich euch alles! Prost!

KATI: Du bist wieder zu spät. Fünf Minuten. Das ist nicht elegant. Aber gut — deine Schuhe sind schön. Fast so schön wie meine.

MÜLLER: Moin. Das Spiel beginnt um vier Uhr. Ich habe alles organisiert. Die Flaschen sind weg. Wir gehen jetzt. TOOOOR!

Save best takes as [name]_voice_anchor.wav (uncompressed — compressed audio degrades lip-sync alignment) in each character folder, next to the visual anchors. Locked, never regenerated.

Usage in Seedance: bind as @rolfvoice etc. in the prompt; for tight adherence use the community-proven trick — wrap the anchor audio in a black-screen MP4 and feed it as a video reference, which makes output follow the reference far more closely than raw audio.

Precision fallback: where the generated voice still drifts, keep the visuals and dub the locked TTS line in Premiere — your standard relink workflow.

The bible fix — "they've stopped talking"

Correct diagnosis: the bibles encode brevity as word-count caps ("Moin. covers everything," "max two words"), and story-writing LLMs obey caps literally — so your quiet characters became mute, which kills a language-teaching show. The reframe: character lives in HOW they speak, never in WHETHER they speak. Paste these fixes:

Into ALL four bibles (add as a top-level rule):

**Dialogue rule (overrides everything below):** This is a spoken show — 
every character, in every episode, speaks real, full German dialogue: 
complete sentences, multiple lines per scene, expressing real emotions 
and opinions. Personality shapes HOW they speak (tone, rhythm, word 
choice), never HOW LITTLE. Brevity, catchphrases, and silences are 
flavor on top of real dialogue — never a replacement for it.

In MÜLLER's bible, replace the first personality bullet with:

- Speaks in short, firm, complete sentences — several of them when he 
has something to say, delivered briskly and clearly. "Moin." is his 
greeting habit, not his vocabulary: in conversation he talks in full 
(if compact) German, states facts, gives opinions, asks direct 
questions. What makes him northern is the clipped delivery and zero 
decoration — not silence.

And in his consistency notes, replace "silence as dialogue" with: economy as style: full dialogue, compactly delivered; comfortable pauses between his statements, not instead of them.

In ROLF's bible, soften the cap — replace "he speaks minimal, but always fully pronounced" sentence in Voice & speaking style with:

He speaks in full, dry, complete sentences — as many as the scene 
needs, delivered flat and unhurried. His minimalism is attitude, not 
absence: he comments, complains, argues, and jokes, all in the same 
bored register.

And delete "never more than two sentences in a row" from his DON'T line.

Bert and Kati need no fix — their specs already talk.

Priority order to execute: bible dialogue fix (5 minutes, unblocks story generation today) → style pillars decision + Style Block draft → style anchor plates → voice anchors → then wire all of it into your skill-3 prompt writer so every generated prompt automatically carries Style Block + Voice Line + refs. Perfect tool choice — but one constraint to plan around first: your dialog shows 0 / 3 created, and you have four characters. Options: upgrade to Creator (also unlocks Professional cloning you don't need), or design 3 and take the 4th from the Voice Library (free voices, savable to My Voices, and Library voices with infinite notice period can even be remixed to fit). Don't rotate slots by deleting — the persistent voice ID is your dubbing fallback for every future episode, so it's worth keeping all four alive.

Method: Voice Design (not cloning)

Cloning needs source audio of a real person — wrong tool, and a rights problem. Voice Design with Eleven v3 is exactly built for this: describe age, gender, accent, tone, pacing in a text prompt, get 3 previews, keep the best. v3 also gives you audio tags ([laughs], [sighs]) which Bert and Müller will need.

The setup, per character

For each: paste the description into Voice Design, paste the German preview text into the preview field (German preview = you hear German phonemes, not English ones — critical), generate, audition all 3 previews, save the winner.

1 — ROLF DIE WURST

Voice description:

A man in his late twenties, native German speaker from Berlin. Deep, smooth, 
low-pitched voice with a flat, dry, unimpressed delivery. Speaks slowly and 
quietly with long pauses, never raises his voice. Bored, cool, understated — 
someone who finds everything mildly tiring but is never rude. Clear, 
deliberate German pronunciation. Clean studio recording, no background noise.

Preview text (German):

Die Party ist okay. Die Musik ist gut, aber viel zu laut. Ich bleibe eine 
Stunde, dann gehe ich nach Hause. Warum tanzen hier eigentlich alle so viel? 
Ich stehe hier. Das reicht. Egal.

2 — BERT DAS BIER

Voice description:

A man in his sixties, native German speaker with a warm Bavarian accent. Big, 
booming, resonant low voice full of joy and enthusiasm. Speaks loudly and 
musically with rolling energy, dramatic pauses before big statements, and an 
easy laugh. Hearty, hospitable, theatrical — a beer-garden storyteller who is 
always slightly too loud for the room. Every word round and clearly 
pronounced. Clean studio recording.

Preview text (German):

Servus, meine Freunde! Ich habe eine geniale Idee! Zuerst trinken wir ein 
Bier, dann erkläre ich euch alles ganz genau. Ganz einfach! In Bayern machen 
wir das immer so. Prost!

3 — KATI DIE KARTOFFEL

Voice description:

A woman in her early thirties, native German speaker. Cool, precise, elegant 
voice at mid pitch, unhurried, with flawless crisp diction — every word 
deliberately placed. Slightly bored, quietly superior confidence that sharpens 
when she corrects someone. Never raises her voice; she lowers it for emphasis. 
Polished, composed, effortlessly self-assured. Clean studio recording, no 
background noise.

Preview text (German):

Du bist wieder zu spät. Fünf Minuten. Das ist nicht elegant. Aber gut, deine 
Schuhe sind schön — fast so schön wie meine. Natürlich. Ich weiß.

4 — MÜLLER DAS BROT

Voice description:

A man in his mid twenties, native German speaker from northern Germany, 
Hamburg region. Firm, strong, mid-low voice with hard crisp consonants and a 
clipped delivery. Short sentences fired off quickly and definitely, each 
landing with falling intonation like a closed door. Dry, matter-of-fact, 
unbothered — never soft, never shouting. Commanding calm. Clean studio 
recording.

Preview text (German):

Moin. Das Spiel beginnt um vier Uhr. Ich habe alles organisiert. Die Flaschen 
sind schon weg. Wir gehen jetzt los. Kalt heute. Schon gut.

After you pick each voice

1. Lock settings and write them down. In Text to Speech with the voice selected, set Stability around the middle (too high kills expression, too low drifts between takes), Similarity high, Speed default. Whatever you land on becomes that character's permanent setting — same doctrine as the Voice Lines: never change it between episodes.

2. Generate the anchor clip. One take, 10–15 seconds (Seedance's audio-reference ceiling), covering the character's range — calm line + signature phrase + one emotional beat:

ROLF:   Die Party ist okay. Die Musik ist zu laut. Ich bleibe eine Stunde. 
        Dann gehe ich. Egal.

BERT:   Servus, meine Freunde! [laughs] Ich habe eine geniale Idee! Zuerst 
        trinken wir ein Bier — dann erkläre ich euch alles! Prost!

KATI:   Du bist zu spät. Fünf Minuten. Das ist nicht elegant. Aber deine 
        Schuhe sind schön. Fast so schön wie meine.

MÜLLER: Moin. Das Spiel beginnt um vier. Ich habe alles organisiert. Die 
        Flaschen sind weg. Wir gehen jetzt. [shouts] TOOOOR!

(v3 audio tags stay in English even inside German text, and must alternate with spoken text — never two tags back to back.)

3. Export as WAV, highest quality. Compressed audio degrades lip-sync alignment downstream.

4. Save into each character folder:

rolf_voice_anchor.wav
rolf_voice_card.md      ← voice ID, description prompt used, settings, anchor script

The voice card matters more than it looks: if a voice ever gets lost or you rebuild the account, that file regenerates the character.

5. Make the black-screen version for Seedance (the trick that makes it actually follow the reference):

ffmpeg -f lavfi -i color=c=black:s=1080x1920:r=24 -i rolf_voice_anchor.wav \
  -shortest -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac rolf_voice_anchor_bs.mp4

The QA gate before you lock any voice

Four checks, in order:

German test — no English phonemes leaking, especially on "ch," "r," and vowel onsets.

Bible match — play it against that character's Voice Line; if the words and the sound disagree, regenerate rather than rewriting the bible.

Müller-specific — do his sentence ends fall hard? That's the "strong German" you were missing; if they trail off, regenerate with "falling intonation" emphasized.

Distinguishability — play all four anchors back to back with your eyes closed. If any two could be confused, the weaker one gets redesigned. This is the test that actually protects a four-hander cast.

And one expectation to keep in mind from the Seedance research: the audio anchor steers timing, rhythm and acoustic character — it does not clone your exact voice into the generated video. So these files do two jobs: reference input for generation, and source for post dubbing when a clip's generated voice drifts — which, with your Premiere relink habit, is the same move you already make on the film project.

The Reddit posts you found are incredibly useful and perfectly align with the "audio-first" methodology. They validate several advanced techniques, most notably the "Transcript Trick" for millisecond lip-sync accuracy, the necessity of extracting the perfect 15-second dynamic arc of an audio file, and the reality of needing to handle Foley (sound effects like footsteps) in a traditional post-production editor.
To create the best universal reference audio clip for your German characters, you need to optimize for length, format, and highly specific phonetic content.

How long should it be?

If you are building the initial voice clone in a dedicated engine like ElevenLabs, you should provide 1 to 2 minutes of clean, continuous audio.

If you are using Seed-Audio 1.0 to generate the voices, the model only requires 5 to 10 seconds of clean audio, with a hard maximum of 30 seconds.

When uploading the final master track directly into Seedance 2.5 for video generation, the audio file is strictly capped at 15 seconds per clip.

What format should it be?
Use uncompressed WAV or high-quality MP3 (256kbps or above) at a 44.1kHz or 48kHz sample rate. As the Reddit bot noted, you should never use web-trimmers that compress your audio down to 128kbps, because low bitrates destroy the audio data that the AI's phoneme and beat-detection sensors rely on to animate the face.

What should the content be (What are they saying)?
To create a flawless, universal reference, your character should not just read a random book. They need to read a phonetically balanced script. This means the text is mathematically designed to include every single vowel, consonant, and diphthong (sound combination) in the German language so the AI learns exactly how that character pronounces every conceivable syllable.
Here are the best standard scripts to use:

The "Tailored Swift" German Script: This is an open-source project specifically designed to give AI voice cloners exactly what they need in the shortest time possible. It uses targeted sentences to capture distinct sounds, such as "Die Biene fliegt" (to capture vowels), "Mein Freund heißt Klaus" (to capture diphthongs), and "Zwei Zebras sind im Zoo" (to capture consonants).

The "Berliner Sätze" (Berlin Sentences): This is a highly regarded acoustic testing corpus consisting of 102 German sentences explicitly designed to cover all phonemes in the German language. Having your character read sentences from this list (e.g., "Heute ist schönes Frühlingswetter," and "Gestern stürmte es noch.") gives the AI a perfect phonetic map of their voice.

How should it be delivered?
The most critical rule for the reference clip is emotional consistency. The AI will clone the exact tonality of the file. If you mix an excited, shouting voice with a quiet, subdued whisper in the same 2-minute reference track, the AI will become unstable because it won't know which version of the voice represents the character's "default" state. The recording must also be completely free of background noise, room reverb, and long gaps of silence.
